problem:
The change-of-coordinates matrix from the basis $B$ to the basis $C$ is given by 
${P}_{B\to C}=[\begin{aligned}\frac{3}{2} & 1 \\ -2 & -1\end{aligned}].$
Find the change-of-coordinates matrix from $C$ to $B$  .

examples.knowledge_point: Using the Invertibility Property of the Change-of-Coordinates Matrix
examples.problem:
The change-of-coordinates matrix from the basis $\mathcal{B}$ to the basis $\mathcal{C}$ is given by 
![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/question-capture-workers/linear/14065461/assets/07a8e394234737d51a0064816b255569d20e826eb3a82884a24f1fc0a9fa6baa.png)
Find the change-of-coordinates matrix from $\mathcal{C}$ to $\mathcal{B}.$
examples.worked_solution:
The change-of-coordinates matrix from $\mathcal{C}$ to $\mathcal{B}$ is the inverse of the change-of-coordinates matrix from $\mathcal{B}$ to $\mathcal{C}.$ Therefore, we simply need to find the inverse of the given matrix.

Computing the inverse of $P_{\small\mathcal{B}\to\mathcal{C}},$ we get

$$
\begin{aligned}{P}_{C\to B} & ={P}_{B\to C}^{-1} \\  & ={[\begin{aligned}-4 & -6 \\ 3 & 5\end{aligned}]}^{-1} \\  & =\frac{1}{(-4)\cdot 5-(-6)\cdot 3}[\begin{aligned}5 & 6 \\ -3 & -4\end{aligned}] \\  & =(-\frac{1}{2})\cdot [\begin{aligned}5 & 6 \\ -3 & -4\end{aligned}] \\  & =[\begin{aligned}-\frac{5}{2} & -3 \\ \frac{3}{2} & 2\end{aligned}].\end{aligned}
$$

feedback.problem:
Let $B={{b}_{1},{b}_{2}}$ be a basis of ${R}^{2}$ and let $S$ be the standard basis of ${R}^{2}.$ 
Find the change-of-coordinates matrix ${P}_{B\to S}$ from $B$ to $S$ if 

$$
{b}_{1}=[\begin{aligned}2 \\ 1\end{aligned}],\,{b}_{2}=[\begin{aligned}1 \\ -1\end{aligned}].
$$
feedback.worked_solution:
Recall  that the standard basis of ${R}^{2}$ consists of the vectors ${e}_{1}$ and ${e}_{2},$ given by

$$
{e}_{1}=[\begin{aligned}1 \\ 0\end{aligned}],\,{e}_{2}=[\begin{aligned}0 \\ 1\end{aligned}].
$$

The components of the vectors of $B$ are just the coordinates relative to the standard basis:

$$
[{b}_{1}]_{S}=[\begin{aligned}2 \\ 1\end{aligned}],\,[{b}_{2}]_{S}=[\begin{aligned}1 \\ -1\end{aligned}]
$$

The change-of-coordinates matrix from $B$ to $S$ is a matrix whose respective columns are the coordinates of the vectors of $B$ relative to the basis $S.$ 

Therefore, we obtain

$$
{P}_{B\to S}=[\begin{aligned}2 & 1 \\ 1 & -1\end{aligned}].
$$
